title: Where to start for a seasoned dev?
author: meshifthenelse
selftext:
I am a software engineer with 10+ years of experience with primarily Python and JavaScript (maybe even some old C). I've built frontend and backend for web applications mainly.

Currently I'm building a diagramming tool for driving AI development (by defining features and guidelines and seeing live the architecture being created with AI).

To cut the story short, I was actually thinking to test my own product by trying to create a game that It would actually like to play. It has to be complex enough but I also want it to be something fun with mechanics and multiplayer so I can play it on my **Nintendo Switch 2.**

The two main 3D game ideas I've had:

\- **Giants: Citizen Kabuto** multiplayer clone.

\- **World War Z horde** mode with slow walking zombies.

Based on LLM response, the recommendation is going with the zombie game for simplicity. And using Unity or Unreal solves the networking from the get go and I can purchase 3D models. The other option is Godot but I'm not sure it would work for a more ambitious game (and unclear on Nintendo porting). Also I haven't used C++ but it feels way too verbose for fast prototyping and readability. So was hoping if there's something simpler looking more like Python so it's faster to go through code (without performance hit). LLM also suggested nodes (no-code), but unsure if that even works with AI.

So to summarize:

1.What engine is best to make porting to Nintendo Switch 2 easy?

2. Which engine makes it seamless for online multiplayer?

3. Fast to read code with less verbosity so you can get the gist.

4. Performant enough if I go with a slow horde defense game.

5. What's the typical timeframe to expect with any of this to get a prototype that works, and then one without major bugs?

6. How would you approach this if you started from fresh? Methodologies, technologies, etc.

7. Anything else I missed?

replies.author: meshifthenelse
replies.body: I've already asked and it seems to keep changing its opinion. Hence here to get an opinion from a human.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
I'm going to tell you the secret. Ready?

Pay attention closely: *It doesn't matter.*

The old rules of "pick the right engine" no longer apply. You need to unlearn the habits of 10+ years of experience because the challenges you were dealing with before no longer apply.

For instance, if you want to port your game to a different engine, that's now just a few prompts away. The most important thing is that you have a game, and so the first place to start is by starting.

Once you fully digest this epiphany, you'll be on your way. Until you don't digest it, you'll still be trapped in the old ways. And that's it. That's all. 

*Just build.*

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body:
If you’re an unknown solo developer, it can be difficult to get your game onto the Nintendo Switch store.
Multiplayer games are several times more difficult than single-player ones. It’s foolish to start with a complex game on a difficult platform. Make something for Steam first.

replies.author: OWazabi
replies.body:
You can definetly get a game going in less than months even  
Thanks god development time was never a true factor on how good a game is :)

But to answer your questions, depending on what your game is, you can get a prototype in a day, or in a few weeks

However you do need to get good at prompting in a way  
and that's not writing good prompts really, but understanding how to properly take advantage of various tools, how to make things in a way that the AI can work a lot by itself efficiently

At first, if you never did stuff like this, you'll probably end up in many situations where you explored a dead end because the AI itself dones't do good there

I recently found a channel that's very good for this, I'd recommend this video  
[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mjg\_JUMar04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mjg_JUMar04)  
(disregard all the part in the beginning where he uses various models, right now just use opus 5.5)  
the video is short, clean, and it demonstrates clearly what type of workflow you need to have  
and he has other good videos about how to make assets and animation, with very good workflows, but the point is understanding the logic behind mostly

Also that other comment that said, ask AI, wasn't that wrong, just ask with more precise specs, and also try  
it's all so new and evolving, get your idea straight, then start trying stuff until finding the pipeline that works for you

comments.author: Excellent-Basket-825
comments.body:
I would start with Godot, especially since you're experienced with Python. Also great to use it with blender.

Use the latest Godot (tell it to use the MCP)  
Use Blender for the models (use the MCP there as well so you can see what it does live)

I think you're overdoing it for your first game with AI, you'll learn a lot in the first one what it does well and what it doesn't. The most important thing is that you learn how to set up improvement loops against references.

For instance: Create concept art with Astra after you've scribbled it on a piece of Paper what you want to do. Then have agent critics loop over it and improve the findings, rerun agent critics.

Especially Opus 5.5 / Sonnet and Astra are extremely good in building against precise specs, which is exactly what a concept art can be if you're detail oriented.  
Hand off the coding, but not the game's soul, it's a lot of work still and you can get through a lot but nail first the core gameplay before you worry about networking.

  
Seriously, just get the base core game loop going that's already hard enough. And \*do not\* skimp or skip good concept art or specification documents. You can use the AI to help create them, but read them through before you submit anything

comments.author: loulo88
comments.body:
I’d de-risk this by separating the experiments. First build a small single-player vertical slice on PC with the core tactical loop; treat Switch 2 as a later porting target, not the constraint that shapes the first prototype. A multiplayer game plus console certification plus AI-assisted production is several unknowns at once, so you won’t know which one caused a failure.

For someone coming from web software, Godot can be a fast way to learn the scene/node model and iterate, while Unity has a larger console and middleware ecosystem. The engine matters less than proving the game loop without networking. Once the loop is fun, add a tiny two-player test with a deliberately narrow map before committing to a full horde mode or a large asymmetric design.
